Its requirements — security planning, periodic risk assessments, assigned responsibilities, control reviews, and incident procedures — go far beyond physical security and are mandatory, not voluntary.
pool.tip: FISMA's reach extends past agencies to the contractors running systems for them.

pool.q: An acquiring organization wants to express its secure development expectations to software suppliers using a shared vocabulary of fundamental practices, and to purchase software built according to those practices. Which NIST publication was created for this?
options: NIST SP 800-88
NIST SP 800-190
NIST SP 800-218, the Secure Software Development Framework (SSDF)
NIST SP 800-160 Volume 2
pool.explanation: SP 800-218 defines the SSDF and explicitly recommends that organizations integrate it into their own practices, express secure development requirements to third-party suppliers using SSDF conventions, and acquire software meeting SSDF practices. SP 800-88 covers media sanitization, SP 800-190 covers container security, and SP 800-160 Vol. 2 addresses engineering cyber-resilient systems.
pool.tip: SSDF (SP 800-218) gives buyer and supplier a common language for secure development.

pool.q: A platform team migrating microservices to containers needs guidance on the security concerns of container technologies, with practical recommendations tied to specific tiers of the container architecture. Which publication is MOST relevant?
options: NIST SP 800-190
ISO/IEC 5055
NIST SP 800-88
ISO/IEC 27701
pool.explanation: NIST SP 800-190, the Application Container Security Guide, explains container-specific security concerns and makes recommendations, many aimed at particular components or tiers of the container technology architecture. ISO 5055 measures internal software structure, SP 800-88 addresses media sanitization, and ISO 27701 covers privacy information management.
pool.tip: Containers → SP 800-190; don't confuse it with general control catalogs.

pool.q: Management wants an international standard for measuring the internal structure of a software product against four critical business factors — security, reliability, efficiency, and maintainability — to judge the system's trustworthiness and resilience. Which standard is this?
options: ISO/IEC 27001
ISO/IEC 5055
ISO/IEC 15288
ISO/IEC 27005
pool.explanation: ISO 5055 measures the internal structure of a software product on security, reliability, efficiency, and maintainability, helping organizations gauge trustworthiness and resilience through integrity and quality measurement. ISO 27001 specifies an ISMS, ISO 15288 describes system life cycle processes, and ISO 27005 guides information security risk management.
pool.tip: ISO 5055 = code-level structural measurement across four business-critical factors.

pool.q: A quality lead notes that the organization still evaluates products against only the six ISO/IEC 9126 characteristics and asks for the modernized successor standard along with what it adds. Which answer is correct?
options: ISO/IEC 25010, which adds security and compatibility
ISO/IEC 27002, which adds confidentiality and availability
ISO/IEC 25010, which adds scalability and portability
ISO/IEC 15288, which adds verification and validation
pool.explanation: ISO 25010 modernizes ISO 9126 and keeps its six characteristics — portability, maintainability, efficiency, usability, reliability, and functionality — while adding security and compatibility. Portability was already part of 9126, so the scalability/portability distractor is wrong, and ISO 27002 is a catalog of security controls, not a product quality model.
pool.tip: 25010 = 9126's six characteristics + security + compatibility.

pool.q: An enterprise that develops software internally, through outsourcers, and in hybrid arrangements wants a multipart standard giving best practices for specifying, designing, selecting, and implementing application security controls through processes integrated across the SDLC, independent of development method. Which standard fits?
options: ISO/IEC 27017
ISO/IEC 9126
ISO/IEC 27034
ISO/IEC 5055
pool.explanation: ISO 27034 provides industry best practice for application security controls through processes woven into the SDLC, is method-agnostic, and applies to internal, external, outsourced, and hybrid development. ISO 27017 supplies cloud implementation guidance for ISO 27001, and the other options are quality and structural measurement standards.
pool.tip: Application security integrated into any style of SDLC → ISO 27034.

pool.q: A multinational preparing for GDPR wants to extend its existing ISO 27001 ISMS with a privacy information management system (PIMS) focused on managing personally identifiable information. Which standard should it adopt?
options: ISO/IEC 27005
ISO/IEC 27018
ISO/IEC 27002
ISO/IEC 27701
pool.explanation: ISO 27701 adds privacy information management guidance on top of ISO 27001, was created with GDPR implementation in mind, and remains adaptable to other privacy regimes. ISO 27018 addresses privacy for cloud service providers specifically, while 27002 and 27005 cover general controls and risk management rather than a PIMS.
pool.tip: 27701 = PIMS extension of 27001; 27018 = cloud-provider privacy code of practice.

pool.q: A security team is directed to classify enterprise data but cannot say where sensitive data resides or what content the organization's many repositories hold. What should the team do FIRST?
options: Deploy data loss prevention agents to all endpoints
Encrypt every repository by default
Perform data discovery to locate data and map where each type resides
Assign security labels to all existing records
pool.explanation: Classification assumes the organization clearly understands what data it possesses, so the first step is data discovery: locating data types and mapping where data resides along with its content. DLP deployment and labeling both depend on classifications that cannot be assigned until discovery establishes the inventory.
pool.tip: Discover, then classify, then label and protect — in that order.

pool.q: A CFO questions why the organization invests effort in classifying its data at all. Which response BEST captures the PRIMARY security benefit of classification?
options: It determines which baseline controls are appropriate for each data set, so strong protections are applied only where warranted and security spending stays cost-effective
It guarantees compliance with every applicable regulation automatically
It eliminates the possibility of insider threats
It transfers legal liability from data owners to data custodians
pool.explanation: Classification lets the organization match baseline safeguards to sensitivity, so expensive measures like strong cryptography and tamper detection are applied where that level of protection is required, achieving cost-effective security. It supports compliance but cannot guarantee it, and it never removes insider risk or shifts the owner's due care accountability.
pool.tip: Classification's payoff: right-sized controls, which means cost-effective protection.

pool.q: A defense contractor stamps "SECRET" in the header and footer of printed documents so staff can apply the correct handling procedures. In NIST terminology, what does this practice describe?
options: Security labeling
Data masking
Steganographic tagging
Security marking
pool.explanation: Security markings associate security attributes with objects in human-readable form, enabling process-based enforcement of security policy — think of marking hard copies. Security labels, by contrast, bind attributes into an information object's data structure so IT systems can enforce policy programmatically.
pool.tip: Marking = human-readable on hard copy; labeling = machine-usable in the data structure.

pool.q: An enterprise is formalizing its data governance roles. Which TWO responsibilities belong to the data owner rather than the data custodian? (Choose two.)
options: Classifying the data according to defined criteria
Performing and restoring backups
Implementing day-to-day security mechanisms
Granting or denying subjects' requests for access to the data
pool.explanation: Data owners — typically business groups — classify data, determine retention requirements, grant or deny access requests, and delegate daily maintenance; they carry the due care accountability for the data. Backups and hands-on security mechanisms are custodian duties performed on the owner's behalf.
pool.tip: Owners decide (classify, approve access); custodians execute (back up, implement controls).

pool.q: In a software development organization, one role is charged with assuring authorized access to data sets, sustaining their integrity, versioning them, and maintaining a history of changes. Which role is this?
options: Data subject
Data custodian
Data owner
Data controller
pool.explanation: The custodian maintains and protects data in custody — backups, security mechanisms, and policy fulfillment — and in a development context this extends to assuring authorized access, sustaining integrity, versioning data sets, and keeping change history. The owner sets classification and access decisions rather than performing maintenance, and controller and subject are privacy roles.
pool.tip: Versioning, backups, and change history are custodial caretaking, not ownership.

pool.q: Under privacy definitions, an individual who can be identified directly or indirectly — for example through an identification number, a telephone number, or an IP address — is called what?
options: A data processor
A data user
A data subject
A data custodian
pool.explanation: The data subject is the person the personal data is about, identifiable directly or indirectly by identifiers or by factors specific to their physical, economic, cultural, or social identity. A data user is an employee who works with data for job tasks, and a processor is a party handling personal data on a controller's behalf.
pool.tip: Subject = the person the data describes; user = the person working with the data.

pool.q: A pipeline ingests JSON and XML files whose embedded metadata is used to catalog and analyze the content. Which general form of data is this?
options: Structured
Semistructured
Unstructured
Binary
pool.explanation: Semistructured data relies on metadata — as in JSON, CSV, or XML — to aid cataloging and analysis, sitting between database-managed structured data and free-form unstructured content. Structured data lives in predefined models such as SQL tables, while unstructured data like video or raw text has no predefined organization.
pool.tip: Metadata-carrying formats (JSON, CSV, XML) are the hallmark of semistructured data.

pool.q: A records manager is drafting a data retention policy. Beyond keeping information needed for operations and regulatory compliance, which pair of objectives should the policy ALSO address?
options: Organizing information so it can be searched and accessed later, and disposing of information that is no longer needed
Maximizing storage utilization and duplicating archives indefinitely
Retaining all data permanently to be safe in litigation
Delegating retention period decisions to individual end users
pool.explanation: A retention policy's objectives are to keep important information for future use, organize it so it can be found and accessed, and dispose of what is no longer needed, balancing legal and business archival demands against storage cost and complexity. Keeping everything forever inverts that balance and worsens both cost and breach exposure.
pool.tip: Retention policy = keep, organize, and dispose — never 'keep everything forever.'

pool.q: An organization is retiring media that stored its most sensitive data classification, and policy states that any residual data remanence is unacceptable. Which disposal approach may be the ONLY acceptable method for this classification?
options: Overwriting the drives with a single pass
Deleting the files and emptying the recycle bin
Reformatting the drives before resale
Physical destruction of the media using approved tools and techniques
pool.explanation: Destruction techniques are chosen per classification — overwriting, purging, or cryptographic erasure may suffice for lower tiers, but for certain sensitivity levels physically destroying the media with appropriate tools is the only acceptable option. Deleting or reformatting leaves recoverable remanence, defeating the requirement.
pool.tip: Highest classification + zero remanence tolerance = destroy the media itself.

pool.q: In a multilevel confidentiality system, a process cleared at Secret attempts to write a file into a Confidential (lower-level) directory, and the operating system blocks the operation. Which Bell-LaPadula rule is being enforced?
options: The simple security property
The star (*) property
The invocation property
The simple integrity property
pool.explanation: Bell-LaPadula's star property permits a subject to save an object only at the same or a higher classification — no write down — precisely to keep high-classification information from leaking to lower levels. The simple security property is 'no read up,' while the simple integrity and invocation properties belong to Biba, an integrity model.
pool.tip: BLP: simple = no read up; star = no write down. Biba flips the directions for integrity.

pool.q: A payments system requires every balance change to follow a strictly defined transaction sequence, forces a second authorized person to evaluate and complete each transaction, and lets subjects touch data only through mediating programs. Which security model do these characteristics implement?
options: Bell-LaPadula
Biba
Clark-Wilson
Graham-Denning
pool.explanation: Clark-Wilson addresses commercial integrity through well-formed transactions, separation of duties in which another party evaluates an authorized subject's transaction before commit, and subject-program-object bindings that remove direct subject access to objects. Biba is also an integrity model but works through lattice levels rather than transaction rules, and Bell-LaPadula addresses confidentiality.
pool.tip: Well-formed transactions + separation of duties + access via programs = Clark-Wilson.

pool.q: A security architect comparing formal models asks which one explicitly governs how subjects and objects are securely created and deleted and how read, grant, delete, and transfer access rights are provisioned, using eight primitive protection rules. Which model is it?
options: Graham-Denning
Brewer and Nash
Bell-LaPadula
Clark-Wilson
pool.explanation: Graham-Denning concerns itself with the basic mechanics other models take for granted: secure creation and deletion of subjects and objects and secure provisioning of read, grant, delete, and transfer rights — eight rules in total. Brewer and Nash prevents conflicts of interest, and Bell-LaPadula assumes subjects and objects already exist and focuses on confidentiality between them.
pool.tip: Eight rules about creating, deleting, and granting = Graham-Denning (HRU is its close cousin).

pool.q: A U.S. online retailer that meets certain thresholds for size and revenue sells to California residents. Which law grants those consumers rights concerning access to, deletion of, and sharing of their personal information, enforceable since July 2020?
options: Gramm-Leach-Bliley Act (GLBA)
California Consumer Privacy Act (CCPA)
Federal Information Security Management Act (FISMA)
Sarbanes-Oxley Act (SOX)
pool.explanation: The CCPA, enacted in 2018 and enforceable as of July 1, 2020, secures privacy rights for California consumers over access, deletion, and sharing of personal information, applying to businesses that meet criteria on size, location, and offerings. GLBA is a federal financial-privacy law without these consumer deletion rights, and FISMA and SOX are not consumer privacy statutes at all.
pool.tip: California consumer rights to access/delete/limit sharing = CCPA.

pool.q: An EU-based SaaS company plans to replicate its customer database to a data center outside the European Union. Which regulation directly imposes conditions and requirements on transferring EU residents' personal data out of the Union?
options: PIPEDA
CCPA
The Australian Federal Privacy Act
The General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR)
pool.explanation: The GDPR, which superseded the 1995 Data Protection Directive, both unifies protection for individuals in the EU and expressly addresses the export of personal data outside the EU, imposing conditions that must be satisfied before such transfers. PIPEDA, CCPA, and the Australian act govern Canadian, Californian, and Australian data respectively.
pool.tip: Cross-border movement of EU personal data is a GDPR question.

pool.q: A Canadian private-sector company collects customer information. Which law requires it to collect, use, or disclose personal information only for purposes that a reasonable person would consider appropriate in the circumstances?
options: Personal Information Protection and Electronic Documents Act (PIPEDA)
Canada's Privacy Act
The OECD privacy principles
California Consumer Privacy Act (CCPA)
pool.explanation: PIPEDA governs Canada's private sector and applies the 'reasonable person' appropriateness test to collection, use, and disclosure of personal information. Canada's Privacy Act is the tempting distractor, but it applies to the government sector and requires PII collection to relate directly to a program or activity of the institution.
pool.tip: Canada: Privacy Act = government sector; PIPEDA = private sector with the reasonable-person test.

pool.q: An app in an OECD member state collects email addresses to send shipping updates, then later uses the same addresses for unrelated advertising without informing anyone. Which OECD privacy principle is MOST directly violated?
options: Personal data should be protected by reasonable security safeguards
Personal data must be accurate, complete, and up to date
Personal data should not be used for purposes other than those specified at the time of collection
Collection should be limited and obtained by lawful means
pool.explanation: The OECD principles require that purposes be specified at collection time and that data not be disclosed or used for other purposes; repurposing shipping emails for advertising breaks exactly that rule. The collection itself was lawful and consensual, so the collection-limitation and safeguards principles are not the ones offended.
pool.tip: Collected for one purpose, used for another = purpose specification/use limitation violation.

pool.q: An organization encrypts personal data at rest, tightly restricts access, and has never suffered a breach, yet a regulator fines it for collecting personal data without consent. What does this outcome illustrate?
options: The encryption must have been implemented incorrectly
Managing cybersecurity risk contributes to but is not sufficient for managing privacy risk, because privacy violations can occur without any security incident
Privacy penalties can only follow a confirmed data breach
Access control has no relevance to privacy protection
pool.explanation: Privacy risk can arise through means unrelated to cybersecurity incidents — such as collecting data without consent — so even flawless security controls cannot by themselves ensure lawful processing. The controls worked as intended; the failure was in privacy compliance, not in encryption or access control.
pool.tip: Perfect security cannot fix unlawful collection: privacy risk ≠ security risk.

pool.q: A dataset of employee names and phone numbers appears twice within a company: once as the department softball roster and once as a list of individuals being treated for an infectious disease. Following NIST guidance, how should sensitivity be judged?
options: Both lists are equally nonsensitive because the data fields are identical
Names and phone numbers can never qualify as PII
Only government-issued identifiers can make PII sensitive
Context determines sensitivity: the treatment list is sensitive PII, and when in doubt PII should be treated as sensitive
pool.explanation: NIST stresses that the context of information matters — the same names and numbers become sensitive PII when tied to medical treatment, since disclosure could cause harm, embarrassment, or stigma. Judging sensitivity purely by field type misses this, and the guidance defaults to treating PII as sensitive when uncertain.
pool.tip: Same fields, different context, different sensitivity — and when unsure, treat PII as sensitive.

pool.q: Before releasing a research dataset, a data engineer introduces small random changes into the numeric values so records no longer exactly match the originals. Which anonymization technique is being applied?
options: Perturbation
Suppression
Generalization
Replacement
pool.explanation: Perturbation anonymizes by making random changes to the data itself. Suppression omits PII fields from the release, generalization swaps specific values for less specific ones (such as birth year instead of full birthdate), and replacement substitutes identifying information — none of which involves injecting random noise.
pool.tip: Random noise = perturbation; omit = suppression; blur detail = generalization; swap = replacement.

pool.q: A supposedly anonymized dataset is published, and a researcher re-identifies individuals by cross-referencing it with a public voter registration file. What is this process called, and what does it demonstrate?
options: Pseudonymization, demonstrating anonymization is reversible by design
Perturbation, demonstrating noise can always be mathematically removed
De-anonymization, demonstrating that anonymized data cannot guarantee privacy because linkage with other data sets may re-identify subjects
Data discovery, demonstrating the publication itself was the only failure
pool.explanation: De-anonymization is the reverse process in which anonymous data is cross-referenced with other sources to re-identify subjects, which is why anonymization never assures complete privacy. Pseudonymization is the tempting confusion, but it refers to data that retains a re-identification code by design, not to an attacker's linkage of released data.
pool.tip: Linkage attacks against released data = de-anonymization risk; anonymization is not absolute.

pool.q: A mobile app presents a consent screen before collecting location data. For the consent to be meaningful, which TWO items must the individual understand? (Choose two.)
options: The application's internal code structure
What data is being collected and why it is being collected
How long the data will be used and how it will be protected
The identities of all other users who consented
pool.explanation: Valid consent requires the individual to understand the purpose, facts, implications, and consequences: what is collected, why and how, how long it will be used, and how it will be protected. Internal implementation details and other users' identities are irrelevant to informed consent — and disclosing other users would itself be a privacy problem.
pool.tip: Consent checklist: what, why, how, how long, and how protected.

pool.q: A call-center application records customer conversations. In some U.S. states one party's consent to recording is enough, while other states require the consent of all parties. What does this variation demand of the team writing the software's requirements?
options: Ignore state law, since federal rules always preempt it
Record video only, never audio, to avoid the issue
Obtain consent from the software vendor before each call
Understand the jurisdictions involved and capture consent requirements that satisfy each applicable one
pool.explanation: Consent obligations vary by jurisdiction — one-party versus all-party recording consent is the classic example — so requirements must reflect every jurisdiction where the software will operate. Assuming federal preemption is wrong here, since states legitimately impose differing recording-consent regimes.
pool.tip: Consent rules are jurisdictional: identify where users are before writing the requirement.

pool.q: An EU user withdraws consent to processing of their personal data, and the controller has no other legal ground to continue. Under GDPR Article 17, what must the controller do?
options: Retain the data for ten years to preserve an audit trail
Anonymize the data and continue using it for marketing
Transfer the data to a processor located outside the EU
Erase the individual's personal data without undue delay
pool.explanation: Article 17, the right to erasure or 'right to be forgotten,' obliges the controller to erase personal data without undue delay when grounds apply, including withdrawal of consent with no remaining legal basis for processing. Continuing any use, retention, or transfer contradicts the erasure obligation once those grounds are met.
pool.tip: Consent withdrawn + no other legal ground = erase without undue delay (GDPR Art. 17).

pool.q: A company operating across several Asia-Pacific economies needs a privacy framework whose Cross-Border Privacy Rules (CBPR) system balances the flow of information across borders with effective protection of personal information. Which framework applies?
options: The APEC Privacy Framework
The EU-U.S. Privacy Shield
The New Zealand Information Privacy Principles
The HIPAA Privacy Rule
pool.explanation: The Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) Privacy Framework requires implementation of the CBPR system, which balances cross-border data flows against personal information protection. Privacy Shield was the EU/Swiss-to-U.S. transfer mechanism, and the NZ IPPs actually make offshore transfers of sensitive information difficult rather than facilitating balanced flows.
pool.tip: CBPR is APEC's mechanism; Privacy Shield is transatlantic.

pool.q: In an attribute-based access control design, testers find that ordinary users can edit the sensitivity attribute stored on records they access, which changes what the authorization engine allows. Why is this a design failure?
options: Attributes should exist only in written policy, never in digital form
Object attributes should be assigned at object creation and subjects must not be able to modify them to manipulate access control decisions
Users should be editing subject attributes instead of object attributes
Sensitivity attributes exist only for audit purposes and never drive access decisions
pool.explanation: Data attributes should be assigned when the object is created and must support logical access decisions with provisions for validation and audit; allowing subjects to alter those attributes lets them manipulate authorization outcomes. Attributes must also stay consistent between digital enforcement and written policy, not be confined to paper.
pool.tip: If a user can rewrite the attribute, the user controls the access decision — never allow it.

pool.q: A security architect concedes it is unrealistic to monitor every data interaction across the enterprise. Which approach BEST reflects sound data access monitoring design?
options: Log every event at maximum verbosity and retain everything indefinitely
Monitor failed login attempts only
Align monitoring, logging, and auditing rigor with the sensitivity of the data and the privileges of the accounts, and deactivate stale accounts such as service accounts idle beyond a defined period
Delegate monitoring responsibility to each end user
pool.explanation: Because total monitoring is infeasible, effort must be proportioned to data sensitivity and account privilege, with metrics aggregated progressively and stale accounts — such as users who miss password changes or service accounts idle past a defined window — deactivated. Blanket maximum logging wastes resources on low-value events while still failing to prioritize what matters.
pool.tip: Monitor in proportion to sensitivity and privilege; idle accounts get deactivated.

pool.q: A team is ready to develop misuse cases for a new application. According to the recommended process, which activity comes FIRST?
options: Develop the use cases for the system
Enumerate misuse cases from identified threats
Create data-flow diagrams of the implementation
Select relevant attack patterns from a catalog
pool.explanation: The process starts with developing use cases, then creating data-flow diagrams for their implementation, then identifying potential threats from the data flows, and finally enumerating misuse cases from those threats using knowledge of attack patterns. Jumping straight to threats or attack patterns skips the system understanding on which the abusive interactions are modeled.
pool.tip: Misuse case pipeline: use cases → DFDs → threats → misuse cases (informed by attack patterns).

pool.q: A security lead proposes writing abuse cases for a checkout feature and is asked to justify the effort. Which TWO outcomes do identified abuse cases directly enable? (Choose two.)
options: Eliminating the need for security testing altogether
Evaluating the business risk associated with each corresponding attack
Determining appropriate safeguards and countermeasures
Guaranteeing the released software contains no vulnerabilities
pool.explanation: Once abuse cases identify specific attacks against the application, teams can evaluate the business risk of each attack, develop security requirements, determine safeguards and countermeasures, and better estimate schedule and resource impact. Abuse cases actually fuel security test creation rather than replace testing, and no technique guarantees vulnerability-free software.
pool.tip: Abuse cases feed risk evaluation, requirements, countermeasures, and test cases — they replace none of them.

pool.q: To ground its misuse cases in real adversary behavior, a team wants a publicly available dictionary of common attack patterns, organized by attack mechanism or domain and developed under the U.S. Department of Homeland Security. Which resource should it consult?
options: MITRE ATT&CK
OWASP ASVS
Common Attack Pattern Enumeration and Classification (CAPEC)
The CVE list
pool.explanation: CAPEC is the DHS-developed public catalog of common attack patterns — entries such as SQL injection, session fixation, and clickjacking — presented by mechanism or domain, ideal for deriving misuse cases. ATT&CK is the tempting distractor, but it is a knowledge base of adversary tactics (the why) and techniques (the how) observed in operations, not a pattern dictionary for requirements work.
pool.tip: CAPEC = attack pattern dictionary (DHS); ATT&CK = adversary tactics and techniques (MITRE).

pool.q: A QA manager takes each completed security test case and maps it back to the security requirement that originated it, confirming no test exists without a requirement. Which SRTM traceability type is being exercised?
options: Forward traceability
Bidirectional traceability
Unilateral traceability
Backward (reverse) traceability
pool.explanation: Backward or reverse traceability maps test cases to requirements, while forward traceability maps requirements to test cases and bidirectional covers both directions at once. 'Unilateral' is not one of the three recognized SRTM traceability types.
pool.tip: Requirements → tests is forward; tests → requirements is backward; both ways is bidirectional.

pool.q: After attackers breached several organizations by exploiting a supplier's weak OAuth integration, a company finalizing a development contract with an offshore supplier reviews its supply chain posture. Which statement BEST describes how software security requirements should be handled in the contract?
options: The supplier should define and impose its own security requirements on the acquiring firm
The acquiring organization should flow its security requirements down to the supplier, establishing expectations up front in the contract
Formal requirements are unnecessary whenever the supplier holds a security certification
Security requirements only become relevant after the first incident occurs
pool.explanation: Because attackers can exploit a weak supplier to reach the acquiring organization — as in the GitHub compromise via third-party OAuth integrators — the acquirer must flow security requirements down to suppliers, with third-party risk assessments verifying the supplier's posture. Well-drafted upfront requirements set expectations early and reduce the need for costly compensating safeguards later; certifications inform but do not replace contractual requirements.
pool.tip: Security requirements flow downhill: from acquirer to supplier (and onward to fourth parties).

pool.q: During threat modeling, a team draws a data flow diagram and pays special attention to the points where the level of trust changes, such as internet-to-web-tier. What are these points called?
options: Data stores
Trust boundaries
External entities
Sequence diagrams
pool.explanation: Trust boundaries are where trust level changes, and threats cluster there, so validation must happen at each crossing. Data stores and external entities are other DFD elements; a sequence diagram is a different model.
pool.tip: Where trust changes = trust boundary; validate at every crossing.

pool.q: In STRIDE, which threat category corresponds to a violation of integrity?
options: Spoofing
Tampering
Repudiation
Denial of service
pool.explanation: In STRIDE, Tampering violates integrity. Spoofing violates authentication, Repudiation violates non-repudiation, and Denial of service violates availability.
pool.tip: STRIDE: Spoofing/auth, Tampering/integrity, Repudiation/non-rep, Info disclosure/confidentiality, DoS/availability, Elevation/authorization.

pool.q: Which threat modeling methodology is a seven-stage, risk-centric process that aligns business objectives with technical threats?
options: STRIDE
PASTA
DREAD
Attack tree
pool.explanation: PASTA (Process for Attack Simulation and Threat Analysis) is a seven-stage, risk-centric methodology. STRIDE is a threat categorization, DREAD is a scoring model, and an attack tree enumerates attack paths.
pool.tip: Seven-stage, risk-centric, business-aligned = PASTA.

pool.q: How must user passwords be stored so that a database breach does not immediately expose them?
options: Encrypted with a symmetric key stored beside them
Hashed with a slow, salted, memory-hard algorithm such as bcrypt, scrypt, or Argon2
Base64-encoded
In plaintext but behind a firewall
pool.explanation: Passwords should be hashed (not encrypted) with a slow, salted, memory-hard function so cracking is expensive and rainbow tables are defeated. Encryption with a nearby key, encoding, and plaintext all leave them recoverable.
pool.tip: Passwords are hashed (bcrypt/scrypt/Argon2 + unique salt), never encrypted.

pool.q: Why does TLS use both asymmetric and symmetric cryptography?
options: Asymmetric is used for bulk data because it is fastest
Asymmetric establishes/exchanges a symmetric session key, then fast symmetric encryption protects the bulk traffic
Symmetric is used only for signatures
It uses hashing instead of encryption
pool.explanation: Asymmetric cryptography is used to securely exchange a symmetric session key (it is too slow for bulk data); symmetric encryption then protects the actual traffic efficiently. This hybrid gets the strengths of both.
pool.tip: Asymmetric for key exchange/signatures; symmetric for bulk data.

pool.q: What does a digital signature provide, and how is it produced?
options: Confidentiality, by encrypting the whole message with a symmetric key
Integrity, authenticity, and non-repudiation, by hashing the message and encrypting the hash with the sender's private key
Availability, by replicating the message
Only compression of the message
pool.explanation: A digital signature hashes the message and encrypts the hash with the sender's private key, giving integrity, authenticity, and non-repudiation. It is verified with the sender's public key. It does not by itself provide confidentiality.
pool.tip: Sign = hash then encrypt hash with the private key; provides integrity + authenticity + non-repudiation.

pool.q: In the cloud shared responsibility model, which items ALWAYS remain the customer's responsibility regardless of service model?
options: The physical data center security
The customer's own data, identity/access management, and configuration
The hypervisor patching
The provider's network backbone
pool.explanation: The customer is always responsible for their data, IAM, and configuration; the provider secures the underlying infrastructure. Misconfigured storage buckets are the classic customer-side failure.
pool.tip: Data, identity, and configuration are always yours in the cloud.

pool.q: Which design principle favors minimizing components shared between different users or processes to avoid unintended information paths?
options: Economy of mechanism
Least common mechanism
Open design
Defense in depth
pool.explanation: Least common mechanism reduces mechanisms shared among users/processes to prevent covert or unintended interactions. Economy of mechanism is about overall simplicity, which is related but distinct.
pool.tip: "Don't share mechanisms between users" = least common mechanism.

pool.q: A team wants recorded TLS traffic to stay safe even if the server's long-term private key is later stolen. Which property should the design provide?
options: Perfect forward secrecy (ephemeral session keys)
Longer RSA keys only
Disabling certificate validation
Client-side caching
pool.explanation: Perfect forward secrecy uses ephemeral per-session keys so a future compromise of the long-term key cannot decrypt previously recorded sessions. Larger keys alone don't provide this, and disabling validation is harmful.
pool.tip: Past traffic safe after key theft = perfect forward secrecy.

pool.q: Which practice reduces a system's attack surface?
options: Enabling every optional feature by default
Disabling unused services, closing unnecessary ports, and removing default accounts
Adding more third-party libraries
Granting all users admin access
pool.explanation: Attack surface reduction removes or restricts entry points: unused services, open ports, and default accounts. Enabling everything, adding libraries, and broad admin access all enlarge the attack surface.
pool.tip: Fewer exposed features/ports/accounts = smaller attack surface.

pool.q: Which two are appropriate uses of hashing (as opposed to encryption)? (Choose 2)
options: Verifying file integrity with a digest
Providing a keyed integrity+authenticity check via HMAC
Reversibly protecting data so it can be decrypted later
Exchanging a session key
pool.explanation: Hashing produces a one-way digest for integrity verification, and HMAC adds a key for integrity plus authenticity. Reversible protection and key exchange are jobs for encryption, not hashing.
pool.tip: Hashing is one-way (integrity); encryption is reversible (confidentiality).

pool.q: A microservices architecture is chosen. Which is a genuine security implication to plan for?
options: There are no network calls to secure
Many service-to-service calls need authentication and encryption (e.g., mutual TLS), and secrets must be distributed securely
Authorization can be ignored between services
The database should be exposed directly to the internet
pool.explanation: Microservices multiply network calls, so each needs authentication and encryption (mutual TLS/service mesh) and secure secret distribution; per-service authorization still matters. Ignoring these or exposing the database directly is unsafe.
pool.tip: More services = more internal calls to authenticate, encrypt, and authorize.

pool.q: A design must protect encryption keys so that they are generated, stored, and used without ever appearing in application memory in plaintext. Which control BEST meets this?
options: A hardware security module or managed key service that performs crypto operations internally
Storing keys in an environment variable on the application host
Embedding keys in a compiled binary to make extraction harder
Encrypting keys with a second key held in the same configuration file
pool.explanation: An HSM or a managed key service holds the key material inside a protected boundary and exposes only operations such as sign, encrypt, and decrypt, so the plaintext key never reaches the application. Environment variables are readable by anything on the host, compiled-in keys are trivially recoverable from the binary, and wrapping a key with another key stored alongside it simply moves the problem one file over.
pool.tip: If the plaintext key must never touch the app, the answer is an HSM or managed key service.

pool.q: A retailer wants to remove primary account numbers from its order and analytics systems entirely, while still allowing those systems to link a customer's repeat purchases. Which approach fits BEST?
options: Tokenization, replacing the PAN with a surrogate value with no mathematical relationship to the original
Encrypting the PAN in every database with a shared application key
Hashing the PAN with an unsalted fast hash
Truncating the PAN to the last four digits everywhere
pool.explanation: Tokenization substitutes a surrogate that carries no derivable relationship to the original value, so the downstream systems keep referential consistency while falling largely out of scope, with the real values held in a hardened token vault. Encryption keeps the value recoverable wherever the key reaches, an unsalted fast hash of a card number is brute-forceable given the small keyspace, and truncation destroys the linkage the retailer needs.
pool.tip: Tokenization removes the sensitive value from scope while preserving referential linkage. Encryption keeps it recoverable.

pool.q: An architecture stops treating the internal network as trusted and instead authenticates and authorizes every request between services on its own merits. Which two statements about this approach are TRUE? (Choose 2)
options: Each service-to-service call must carry verifiable identity and be authorized independently
Network location alone is no longer sufficient grounds to grant access
A perimeter firewall becomes unnecessary and can be removed
Once a client authenticates at the edge, internal calls can be trusted implicitly
pool.explanation: Zero trust replaces implicit network trust with per-request verification, so every internal hop authenticates and is authorized on its own. Being inside the network proves nothing. Perimeter controls still add value as one layer among many, and implicit trust of internal calls after an edge authentication is precisely the assumption zero trust removes.
pool.tip: Zero trust means never trust, always verify, on every hop, not just at the edge.

pool.q: A multinational insurer is losing track of how its data, processes, locations, people, timing, and motivations relate as the business changes. An enterprise architect proposes classifying the existing organization in a two-dimensional, 36-cell matrix whose columns ask what, how, where, who, when, and why, and whose rows move from the planner's view down through owner, designer, implementer, and subconstructor to the user's view. Which framework is the architect PRIMARILY describing?
options: TOGAF
SABSA
The Zachman Framework
ITIL
pool.explanation: The Zachman Framework is a classification schema for enterprise architecture built as a 6x6 matrix: six interrogative columns crossed with six stakeholder perspectives, used to model existing functions while controlling business change. SABSA shares a similar layered layout but is a risk-driven security architecture with its own layer names, and TOGAF and ITIL are a development method and a service management practice, respectively, not a 36-cell classification grid.
pool.tip: Six questions times six perspectives equals 36 cells - that grid is always Zachman.

pool.q: A newly hired CISO wants the security architecture to be driven by business risk, with guidance for ongoing service management, and structured in six layers - contextual, conceptual, logical, physical, component, and operational - each mapped to a stakeholder perspective from business owner to manager. Which framework BEST fits this description?
options: SABSA
The Zachman Framework
COBIT
The NIST Cybersecurity Framework
pool.explanation: Sherwood Applied Business Security Architecture (SABSA) is a risk-based enterprise security architecture that includes service management guidance and stacks six layers from contextual down to operational, each tied to a perspective. Zachman inspired a similar row-per-perspective structure but is a general classification matrix rather than a security-specific, risk-driven model, and COBIT and the NIST CSF are governance and cybersecurity outcome frameworks, not layered security architectures.
pool.tip: Risk-driven security layers ending in 'operational/management' point to SABSA; a question-word grid points to Zachman.

pool.q: An integration team is choosing a web service approach for a new customer-facing platform. One stated requirement is that services be fast and lightweight and be able to exchange JSON payloads rather than being locked into a single message format. Which statement about the candidate approaches is TRUE?
options: SOAP is an architectural style that can carry JSON, while REST is a protocol bound to XML
Both SOAP and REST are protocols that strictly require XML for message transport
REST is a protocol that mandates JSON, so it cannot interoperate with XML-based systems
REST is an architectural style supporting multiple formats such as JSON, while SOAP is a protocol that relies strictly on XML
pool.explanation: REST is an architectural style, not a protocol, and it permits various representations including JSON, which is why RESTful services tend to be simple, fast, and lightweight. SOAP is a protocol and strictly depends on XML for message transport, so the options that reverse the two or claim both require XML - or that REST forbids XML - misstate the distinction.
pool.tip: SOAP = Protocol + XML only; REST = style + any format (JSON welcome).

pool.q: A team is building a native mobile application that must let users grant it limited access to files held by a third-party service without ever handing over their credentials. The design calls for issuing access tokens over HTTPS with JSON payloads, and it addresses only authorization, not authentication. Which standard is the team MOST likely selecting?
options: SAML
OAuth
Kerberos
XACML
pool.explanation: OAuth is an open standard for authorization only: it grants devices, APIs, and servers access tokens instead of credentials, works over HTTPS, typically carries JSON rather than XML, and addresses SAML's shortcomings on mobile platforms. SAML performs both authentication and authorization using XML assertions between an identity provider and service provider, Kerberos is a ticket-based network authentication protocol, and XACML is a policy language rather than a token-issuing authorization standard.
pool.tip: Tokens-not-credentials, JSON, HTTPS, mobile-friendly, authorization only - that recipe spells OAuth.

pool.q: In a defense contractor's document system, a central policy authority assigns access rights to every file. An engineer who authors a design document discovers she cannot grant a teammate access to it herself; only the central authority can change the policy. Which access control model MOST precisely describes this system?
options: Discretionary access control (DAC)
Role-based access control (RBAC)
Nondiscretionary access control (NDAC)
Mandatory access control (MAC)
pool.explanation: Under MAC, access policy decisions are made by a central authority and the object's owner cannot alter the rights, which is exactly the scenario. DAC is the opposite - the owner or another authorized party decides who may access the object - and RBAC assigns permissions through job roles, which is not stated here. NDAC is the broader category of controls not set at user discretion, so MAC is the more precise answer.
pool.tip: Owner powerless plus central authority in charge = MAC; owner decides = DAC.

pool.q: A payment gateway validates client certificates before accepting transactions. Operations reports that downloading and processing the published lists of revoked certificates is slow, and the lists are sometimes out of date, letting a recently revoked certificate slip through. Which change BEST addresses these shortcomings?
options: Query each certificate's revocation status on demand using OCSP
Cache the certificate revocation lists locally for a longer period
Replace CA-issued certificates with self-signed certificates
Disable revocation checking and rely on short TLS session lifetimes
pool.explanation: The Online Certificate Status Protocol was designed to address exactly these CRL weaknesses: lists that grow long and time-consuming to process and that may be stale, whereas OCSP checks a single certificate's current status when needed. Caching CRLs longer makes staleness worse, self-signed certificates remove trusted third-party validation entirely, and skipping revocation checking leaves revoked certificates accepted.
pool.tip: When the complaint is 'long, slow, or stale revocation lists,' the fix is OCSP.

pool.q: A hosting provider builds virtualization servers in which the virtualization layer is installed directly on the physical hardware, with no general-purpose operating system beneath it, and its main job is sharing hardware among several guest operating systems. Which statement about this design is TRUE?
options: It is a Type 2 hypervisor, because every hypervisor depends on a host operating system
It is a container engine, since the guests share the hardware's single kernel
It is a Type 1 hypervisor, also called a native, embedded, or bare-metal hypervisor
It is a Type 1 hypervisor, which is why it can only run guests from one OS family
pool.explanation: A Type 1 hypervisor - known as bare-metal, native, or embedded - runs directly on the host hardware and manages the guest operating systems above it. A Type 2 hypervisor is the one installed on top of a conventional operating system and is completely dependent on that host OS, and it is containers, not hypervisor guests, that share one kernel and are tied to a single OS family.
pool.tip: No host OS underneath means bare metal, and bare metal means Type 1.

pool.q: An architect is moving a suite of microservices from virtual machines to containers running on a shared host to cut resource overhead. When assessing the security of this change, which isolation characteristic MUST the architect account for?
options: Each container ships with its own complete guest operating system, preserving VM-grade isolation
All containers share the host's OS kernel, so they are segregated at the software level and must match the host's OS family
A hypervisor gives each container hardware-level isolation identical to a virtual machine
A kernel compromise on the host is contained to a single affected container
pool.explanation: Containers share the host operating system's kernel and are segregated from one another in software, which also means a Linux host runs only Linux containers and a Windows host only Windows containers. It is virtual machines that carry a full guest OS and receive hardware-level isolation from a hypervisor, and because the kernel is shared, compromising it endangers every container on the host rather than just one.
pool.tip: Containers share the kernel; VMs bring their own OS - weaker isolation, same OS family.

pool.q: Researchers demonstrate that they can recover secret keys from a vendor's cryptographic module by measuring its power consumption and the timing of its operations, without ever physically opening or modifying the device. Which design change would BEST mitigate this class of attack?
options: Implement constant execution time and stabilize the module's characteristic signatures for sensitive operations
Move the keys into a TPM and double the key length
Require TLS for all traffic between the module and calling applications
Add tamper-evident seals and hardened casing to the module
pool.explanation: This is a side-channel attack, which exploits physical leakage such as timing, power draw, and electromagnetic or acoustic emissions; the recognized defenses in cryptographic modules are constant execution time and stabilized signatures for sensitive operations, and FIPS 140 requires testing against such noninvasive attacks. Longer keys and TLS protect data and transport, not physical emissions, and tamper seals counter invasive physical attacks, whereas side channels need no physical intrusion at all.
pool.tip: Leaks through timing or power are fixed by making operations look identical - constant time, stable signatures.

pool.q: A software team is preparing to deploy a new application to a public cloud provider. The security lead reminds them that regardless of the service model or deployment model ultimately chosen, two overarching risks apply to any application run in the cloud and must always be weighed. Which two risks is the lead referring to? (Choose two.)
options: Vendor lock-in
Multitenancy
Third-party administration
Loss of source code escrow
pool.explanation: Developers must always keep in mind that cloud workloads share underlying infrastructure with other customers (multitenancy) and that the provider, not the customer, administers that underlying environment (third-party administration); both risks shape security requirements across every service and deployment model. Vendor lock-in is a business and portability concern rather than the ever-present security pairing, and source code escrow relates to supplier continuity, not cloud runtime risk.
pool.tip: Cloud's two constants: strangers on your hardware (multitenancy) and strangers running it (third-party admin).

pool.q: A security architect at a global logistics firm is adopting SABSA to build a risk-driven security architecture. Management asks how the framework structures work over time. Which set of life cycle phases does SABSA define?
options: Initiation, Development, Operations, and Disposal
Plan, Do, Check, and Act
Strategy and Planning, Design, Implementation, and Management and Measurement
Preparation, Categorization, Selection, and Authorization
pool.explanation: SABSA's life cycle consists of Strategy and Planning, Design, Implementation, and Management and Measurement, reflecting its risk-based, business-driven approach that includes ongoing service management. Plan-Do-Check-Act is the Deming quality cycle and Preparation/Categorization belong to the NIST RMF, both commonly confused with architecture frameworks.
pool.tip: SABSA = business risk driven; remember its four phases end with Management and Measurement, showing it covers operations, not just design.

pool.q: A facility's CCTV system discourages would-be intruders who see the cameras, and its recordings are also reviewed to spot break-ins after the fact. What does this arrangement BEST illustrate about security controls?
options: A single control can provide more than one function, such as deterrence and detection
CCTV is an administrative control because it supports management oversight
Physical controls always outperform technical controls for intrusion handling
Deterrent controls are a subcategory of corrective controls
pool.explanation: Controls are categorized by the functions they provide (prevent, deter, detect, delay, correct, recover), and one control such as CCTV can serve multiple functions at once, here deterring and detecting. Defense in depth would involve layering several different controls, whereas this scenario is one control performing two roles; CCTV is a physical/technical safeguard, not an administrative one.
pool.tip: Classify controls by nature (physical, administrative, technical) AND by function - one control can serve several functions.

pool.q: An organization replaces a centralized mainframe application with a client-server design in which desktop clients call a central application server. From a security standpoint, what is the PRIMARY consequence of this architectural shift?
options: Authentication becomes unnecessary because the server enforces all policy
The attack surface expands because adversaries can target the client, the server, or the communication channel
Availability improves automatically because clients cache all business data
The design eliminates the need for network security protocols
pool.explanation: Compared to centralized computing, client-server architecture gives attackers three broad targets: the client component, the server component, and the channel between them, which expands the attack surface. The distractors invert the reality - moving to client-server increases, rather than removes, the need for authentication and secure transport.
pool.tip: Every added component or communication path in a distributed design is another attack target.

pool.q: During a design review of an n-tier enterprise web application, the team catalogs threats tier by tier. Which threat is characteristically associated with the WEB tier rather than the business logic or persistence tiers?
options: Insecure storage of records
Buffer overrun in processing routines
Command injection in back-end services
Poor session management and path traversal
pool.explanation: Web-tier threats include poor session management, parameter manipulation, path traversal and disclosure, canonicalization, and URL encoding issues, all tied to handling of requests at the presentation boundary. Buffer overruns and command injection are catalogued at the business logic tier, and insecure storage belongs to the persistence tier.
pool.tip: Map threats to tiers: session/URL/path issues at the web tier, injection and logic flaws in the middle, storage flaws at the data tier.

pool.q: A startup is designing a peer-to-peer file sharing network where every node can both request and serve files with no central server. Given how attackers typically abuse such networks, which design control is MOST important to include?
options: A master-and-slave configuration so one program controls the others
Strong access control to prevent uploads of malicious files from untrusted sources
Caching proxies at every peer to improve response time
A central resource manager that assigns roles to each peer
pool.explanation: P2P file sharing networks are well-known channels for implanting malware, so designs must include strong access control that blocks uploads from untrusted sources. A master-and-slave configuration and central resource management describe client-server designs and contradict the defining trait of P2P, where responsibilities are spread uniformly and each peer acts as client and server.
pool.tip: P2P has no central authority, so trust and upload controls must be built into every peer.

pool.q: An architecture uses a message queue so independent producer and consumer services can communicate asynchronously. Which two protections MOST directly address the security aspects specific to this design? (Choose two.)
options: Encrypting the message body while messages sit in the queue
Converting the design to synchronous request-response calls
Restricting which identities may access the queue
Relying on the network perimeter firewall to protect queued data
pool.explanation: For message queuing, the two highlighted concerns are protecting the messages themselves, such as encrypting the message body in the queue, and restricting access to the queue. Forcing synchronous calls removes the architectural benefit without adding protection, and perimeter firewalls do nothing for messages at rest inside the queue infrastructure.
pool.tip: For queues, think protect the message AND protect the queue - encryption plus access restriction.

pool.q: A banking API returns account records based on an account identifier supplied in the request. A tester logs in with a low-value account, changes the identifier in the URL, and retrieves another customer's account data. Which OWASP API Security Top 10 risk does this demonstrate?
options: Broken Object Level Authorization
Broken Function Level Authorization
Broken Authentication
Security Misconfiguration
pool.explanation: When an endpoint uses a client-supplied ID to reach a data source without verifying the caller is entitled to that specific object, the flaw is Broken Object Level Authorization, which requires object-level checks in every function that accesses data by user-supplied ID. Broken Function Level Authorization concerns access to entire functions such as admin operations, not individual data objects, and authentication itself succeeded here.
pool.tip: Swapping an ID to reach someone else's record = object-level authorization failure, the number one API risk.

pool.q: A concert ticketing API works exactly as specified, yet scalpers use automated scripts to buy out entire events within seconds, harming legitimate customers. According to the OWASP API Security Top 10, which risk BEST describes this exposure?
options: Server Side Request Forgery
Unrestricted Access to Sensitive Business Flows
Broken Object Property Level Authorization
Improper Inventory Management
pool.explanation: Unrestricted Access to Sensitive Business Flows occurs when an API exposes a business process, like purchasing tickets, without compensating for the harm of excessive automated use; notably, it does not require an implementation bug. Unrestricted Resource Consumption or SSRF involve technical resource abuse or coerced requests, whereas here the code functions correctly but the business flow is abused.
pool.tip: If the API 'works as designed' but automation wrecks the business, think sensitive business flows, not a coding bug.

pool.q: An API accepts a user-supplied URL for fetching a profile image from the web. An attacker submits an internal address, and the API server, sitting behind the corporate firewall, dutifully requests that internal resource and returns the response. Which API risk is being exploited?
options: Unsafe Consumption of APIs
Unrestricted Resource Consumption
Server Side Request Forgery
Broken Object Level Authorization
pool.explanation: Server Side Request Forgery arises when an API fetches a remote resource without validating the user-supplied URI, letting an attacker coerce the server into sending crafted requests to unexpected destinations, even ones protected by a firewall or VPN. Unsafe Consumption of APIs concerns trusting data from third-party services, not being tricked into issuing requests on an attacker's behalf.
pool.tip: User controls the URL the server fetches = SSRF; the server's position inside the perimeter is what makes it valuable.

pool.q: A development team integrates a third-party address-verification API and passes its responses directly into SQL queries, reasoning that a reputable partner's data needs no validation. Attackers later compromise the partner service and inject malicious payloads through it. Which OWASP API Security Top 10 risk did the team's assumption create?
options: Security Misconfiguration
Broken Authentication
Server Side Request Forgery
Unsafe Consumption of APIs
pool.explanation: Unsafe Consumption of APIs describes developers trusting data from third-party APIs more than user input and applying weaker standards to it, which lets attackers strike through integrated services instead of attacking the target directly. Security Misconfiguration involves flawed settings on the API's own stack, not misplaced trust in a partner's data.
pool.tip: Treat third-party API responses like any untrusted input - attackers pivot through your integrations.

pool.q: A payment platform must remain reachable through hardware failures, so architects propose a deployment with additional nodes and multiple running instances of key processes. Which deployment characteristic does this design PRIMARILY provide?
options: A smaller attack surface than a single-server deployment
Simplified security management through consolidation
Built-in redundancy with automatic failover
Elimination of the need for backup procedures
pool.explanation: High availability is a special type of multinode deployment that uses extra nodes and multiple instances of key processes to deliver built-in redundancy and automatic failover. Simplified security management is a benefit of the single-server model, and adding nodes generally enlarges rather than shrinks the attack surface; redundancy also never replaces backups.
pool.tip: Single server = simplest to manage; distributed = reliability; high availability = redundancy + automatic failover.

pool.q: A rich internet application performs elaborate validation and authorization logic in JavaScript within the browser to give users instant feedback. Which statement BEST reflects the secure design position on this approach?
options: Client-side checks are acceptable for user experience, but every validation, authorization, and authentication decision must be enforced again at the server
Client-side checks are sufficient when the JavaScript is minified and obfuscated
Authorization may remain client-side as long as authentication is server-side
Client-side validation should be removed entirely because it serves no purpose
pool.explanation: RIA logic runs in the user's domain where it can be disabled or bypassed, so the client may validate to save round trips, but all validation, authorization, and authentication must be backed by the server. Obfuscation only slows an attacker and does not restore trust, and removing client validation entirely discards a legitimate usability and performance aid.
pool.tip: Anything running in the browser belongs to the user - client checks are convenience, server checks are security.

pool.q: A vendor of smart cameras maps its product risks to NIST's high-level IoT risk mitigation goals. Preventing a camera from being conscripted into a distributed denial of service botnet or used to eavesdrop on neighboring network traffic falls under which goal?
options: Protect individuals' privacy
Protect device security
Protect data security
Protect supply chain integrity
pool.explanation: NISTIR 8228 frames IoT risk around three goals, and preventing a device from being used to conduct attacks, including DDoS participation and eavesdropping on the network segment, is the essence of protecting device security, which applies to all IoT devices. Protecting data security covers the confidentiality, integrity, and availability of data the device handles, and privacy protection addresses PII processing impacts beyond those two.
pool.tip: NIST IoT goals: device security (don't be a weapon), data security (protect the data), privacy (protect people).

pool.q: A retailer issues employee badges containing passive RFID tags and worries that adversaries with rogue readers could wirelessly harvest badge data from outside secure rooms. Which mitigation BEST addresses this shielding concern?
options: Extending the tag read range for faster scanning
Switching the badges to broadcast over Wi-Fi
Deploying a web application firewall at the perimeter
Using Faraday cage shielding to prevent signal penetration
pool.explanation: Rogue, unauthorized RFID readers are a recognized risk, and Faraday cages are the cited mitigation for shielding tags and preventing signal penetration. A WAF protects web traffic and is irrelevant to RF emissions, while extending read range or moving to Wi-Fi would enlarge the wireless exposure rather than reduce it.
pool.tip: RFID risks are about unwanted RF reads - shield the signal (Faraday cage), don't just harden the network.

pool.q: A design team adds tap-to-pay functionality using near-field communication, arguing that because NFC only works across a few centimeters, protecting the exchanged data is unnecessary. What is the BEST response to this reasoning?
options: Close proximity does remove the need for encryption, but only for payment data
NFC transactions cannot be secured because the protocol lacks any cryptographic support
Encryption should still be used where possible because implementation flaws and short-range interception can lead to compromise
The team should replace NFC with RFID, which is inherently secure
pool.explanation: Although NFC data exchange is limited to short distances, flaws in the implementation of the technology can still create exploitable vulnerabilities, so encryption should be applied to the data exchange where possible. Distance is a constraint on the attacker, not a security control, and RFID shares the same class of wireless exposure rather than fixing it.
pool.tip: Short range shrinks the attack window but is never a substitute for encrypting the data.

pool.q: A utility deploys a network of small environmental sensor nodes that relay readings to a central processing site. Which pair of issues is MOST commonly highlighted as the general security concern for such sensor networks?
options: Reliability and trustworthiness of the sensors, and confidentiality of the data
Excessive battery life and oversized processors
License compliance and source code escrow
Physical size of the nodes and cable management
pool.explanation: For sensor networks, the reliability and trustworthiness of the sensors themselves and the confidentiality of the data they transmit are the concerns usually highlighted, since decisions are made centrally on data gathered by many small, exposed nodes. The other options describe logistical or licensing matters rather than the security properties of the sensed data pipeline.
pool.tip: Sensor networks: can you trust what the node reports, and can anyone else read it in transit?

pool.q: An engineer claims the code in the company's smart thermostat is firmware because it runs on a small device. Which statement CORRECTLY distinguishes embedded software from firmware?
options: Embedded software always requires direct user interaction, while firmware never executes
Firmware typically hands control over to other software such as an operating system, whereas embedded software may be the only code that runs on the device
Firmware is stored in RAM, while embedded software lives only in the cloud
Embedded software and firmware are interchangeable terms with no distinction
pool.explanation: The distinction is that firmware normally passes control to another piece of software such as the OS after doing its job, while embedded software may be the sole code running on the hardware, controlling its limited function set without direct user interaction. The terms are related but not interchangeable, and neither definition hinges on RAM versus cloud storage.
pool.tip: Firmware boots and hands off; embedded software can be the whole show on the device.

pool.q: A defense supplier ships field-programmable gate arrays in equipment that may fall into hostile hands. Compared to custom application-specific integrated circuits, what security concern does the FPGA's defining characteristic introduce MOST directly?
options: FPGAs cannot perform cryptographic operations of any kind
FPGAs are manufactured with fixed logic that can never be altered
Because FPGAs are programmable after manufacturing, adversaries may clone the intellectual property, tamper with the application, or introduce malware
FPGAs consume so much power that side channels are impossible to measure
pool.explanation: FPGAs are programmed to desired functionality after manufacturing, unlike ASICs that are custom built for a fixed task, and that programmability creates concerns about copying or cloning intellectual property, tampering to disable features or leak information, introducing malware, and malicious reuse of the device itself. The fixed-logic description belongs to ASICs, which is exactly the property FPGAs lack.
pool.tip: FPGA = reprogrammable in the field, so protect the design (IP) and the configuration, not just the data.

pool.q: A software company with development teams in four countries needs everyone to build and test a new product inside one shared, rented environment with virtualized servers, without buying hardware or managing operating systems themselves. Which cloud service model fits this need BEST?
options: Software as a Service
Infrastructure as a Service
Community cloud
Platform as a Service
pool.explanation: PaaS lets customers rent virtualized servers and associated services for developing and testing new applications, and a highlighted benefit is that geographically scattered development teams can work together within the same environment. IaaS would leave the team provisioning and managing infrastructure components themselves, SaaS delivers a finished application rather than a build environment, and community cloud is a deployment model, not a service model.
pool.tip: Developers collaborating in a rented build/test environment = PaaS; raw provisioned infrastructure = IaaS.

pool.q: A tax-preparation company runs its core systems in a private cloud but experiences enormous demand spikes each filing season. Architects propose keeping steady-state workloads on-premises and overflowing into a public cloud only during the peak. Which deployment model does this describe?
options: Community cloud
Hybrid cloud
Public cloud with dedicated tenancy
Private cloud with high availability
pool.explanation: Combining on-premises or private cloud infrastructure with public cloud, including bursting out of the private cloud into the public cloud during peak demand such as tax season, is the definition of a hybrid cloud. A community cloud is a multitenant environment shared by organizations with similar needs, which does not capture the burst-on-demand pattern described.
pool.tip: 'Burst to public during peaks, private the rest of the time' is the textbook hybrid cloud scenario.

pool.q: A cloud security assessment ranks components by exposure. Which statement about the cloud management plane is MOST accurate?
options: It only renders billing dashboards and poses negligible risk
It is the most powerful tool in the cloud infrastructure, is used by the most privileged users, and its components carry the highest risk from software vulnerabilities
It is reserved exclusively for tenants and is never touched by provider personnel
It handles only physical rack maintenance and cabling records
pool.explanation: The management plane creates, starts, and stops virtual machine instances and provisions their resources, making it the most powerful tool in the entire cloud infrastructure; it is used by the most privileged users, integrates authentication, access control, and logging, and its components are at the highest risk concerning software vulnerabilities. It serves both provider administrators and tenants with controlled access, so the exclusivity claims in the other options are wrong.
pool.tip: Whoever controls the management plane controls the cloud - treat it as the crown jewel of cloud security.

pool.q: An engineer needs cloud storage that can be attached to an infrastructure-as-a-service virtual machine instance and behave exactly like a physical hard drive hosting a file system. Which storage type meets this requirement?
options: Object storage accessed through web interfaces
Network-attached storage serving files over SMB
Volume storage
A storage area network's tape library tier
pool.explanation: Volume storage is a virtual hard drive that can be attached to a virtual machine instance and used to host a file system, with writes going to committed blocks so it behaves just like a physical drive or array. Object storage instead keeps unstructured data as objects with metadata reached through programming or web interfaces, and NAS is a file-level server on a network rather than an attachable virtual disk.
pool.tip: Volume = virtual disk for a VM (block); object = metadata-rich units via API; NAS = file-level; SAN = block-level network.

pool.q: A penetration test of a mobile banking app finds that account statements are cached on the handset in plaintext files that any app with storage access can read. In the OWASP Mobile Top 10, which category BEST fits this finding?
options: Insecure data storage
Insecure communication
Improper platform usage
Reverse engineering
pool.explanation: Sensitive data written unprotected to the device's local storage is the classic Insecure Data Storage weakness (M2), because the flaw lies in how data at rest on the handset is kept. Insecure communication concerns data in transit between client and server, and improper platform usage refers to misusing OS features or platform security controls rather than storing data carelessly.
pool.tip: Mobile findings: at rest on the device = M2; in transit = M3; misused OS feature = M1.

pool.q: After the Meltdown and Spectre disclosures, a developer asks why a processor performance feature can leak secrets. Which explanation is MOST accurate?
options: The processor broadcasts all instructions over the management network
Modern processors have no memory protection between processes
Branch predictors encrypt data with keys that attackers already know
Speculatively executed instructions can leave residue of sensitive information in cache or memory that side-channel techniques can then recover
pool.explanation: With speculative execution, the microprocessor runs upcoming instructions ahead of time, and even abandoned speculative paths can leave traces of sensitive information in cache or memory that attackers extract using side-channel methods; disabling speculative execution is the cited mitigation. The other options misstate how processors work - the issue is measurable residue, not broadcast data or absent memory protection.
pool.tip: Meltdown/Spectre = speculation leaves cache footprints; side channels read the footprints.

pool.q: An automotive supplier must generate, store, and use cryptographic keys inside each vehicle's electronic control units, using a hardware element integrated directly into the device. Which technology is designed for this purpose?
options: A certificate revocation list
A network-attached storage appliance
An embedded hardware security module
A software-defined network controller
pool.explanation: Embedded hardware security modules are hardware elements integrated into digital devices to perform cryptographic functions, and they are specifically designed for use in IoT devices and automotive security. A CRL only lists revoked certificates and provides no key storage, while NAS and SDN controllers address storage and networking rather than protected key life cycle management.
pool.tip: eHSM = HSM shrunk and soldered into the device - the go-to answer for IoT and automotive key protection.

pool.q: A data science team feeds a large set of customer transactions into an algorithm without any labels, hoping the system will discover natural groupings of purchasing behavior on its own. Which machine learning category are they using?
options: Supervised learning
Unsupervised learning
Reinforcement learning
Semisupervised learning
pool.explanation: Unsupervised learning uses unlabeled data to detect categories within it, which matches discovering customer groupings without predefined labels. Supervised learning requires labeled training data to build a predictive model, reinforcement learning relies on trial and error guided by rewards, and semisupervised learning mixes labeled and unlabeled data.
pool.tip: No labels, find the clusters = unsupervised; labels = supervised; rewards = reinforcement.
